subject: Chemistry
title: Chlorine Trifluoride: Burns Anything
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Chlorine Trifluoride: Burns Anything.

hook.text: Chlorine trifluoride is so reactive it sets fire to glass, sand, water, and even asbestos.

buildup.text: It's a stronger oxidizer than oxygen itself. Materials that can't normally burn will ignite on contact.

discovery.text: Nazis tried to use it as a weapon. It was too dangerous—it corroded its own storage containers.

twist.text: A spill at a factory once burned through 30 cm of concrete and a meter of gravel beneath it.

climax.text: It's still used in tiny amounts to clean semiconductor equipment. Handle with extreme caution.

punchline.text: Burns glass, concrete, and water. Chemistry's most terrifying liquid.

quiz.question: What makes chlorine trifluoride so dangerous?
options: It is a stronger oxidizer than oxygen and ignites almost any material
It explodes when exposed to air

details.summary: Chlorine trifluoride is one of the most reactive chemicals known, capable of igniting materials that are normally fireproof including glass, sand, asbestos, and even water. This hypergolic oxidizer is so aggressive that it was considered too dangerous for use as rocket fuel.
details.whyItMatters: ClF3 demonstrates the extremes of chemical reactivity and the fluorine atom's extraordinary oxidizing power. Its story is a cautionary tale in industrial chemistry safety.
takeaways: ClF3 can ignite water, glass, sand, and asbestos on contact
It was deemed too dangerous even for military rocket applications
Fluorine's extreme electronegativity drives its reactive power

faq.question: How can a chemical set water on fire when water is used to extinguish fires?
faq.answer: Chlorine trifluoride is a stronger oxidizer than oxygen itself. It rips hydrogen atoms from water molecules violently, releasing energy and producing hydrofluoric acid and oxygen. The reaction is so energetic that it ignites the hydrogen, making water combust.

faq.question: Was chlorine trifluoride ever actually used as rocket fuel?
faq.answer: It was tested as a rocket oxidizer by both the US and Nazi Germany. While its performance was excellent, containment proved nearly impossible because it corroded most materials. A famous spill at a test facility burned through concrete, gravel, and a meter of dirt.
